## About this report

The data is IBGE's **PMC** (*Pesquisa Mensal do Comércio*): the sales volume index of
**expanded retail** (which includes vehicles and construction materials), by state (UF),
monthly from January 2004, base 2022 = 100, **without seasonal adjustment**.

The analysis follows the course workflow (`aulas/fundamentos.qmd`, `aulas/arima.qmd`,
`aulas/sarima-prophet.qmd`): look at the data, test for unit roots, identify, fit
`AutoARIMA(season_length=12)`, check the residuals, and forecast 24 months ahead with
80% and 95% intervals.

The state is a **parameter**. To render the report for another UF:

```bash
uv run quarto render template-exercicio-sarima.qmd -P UF:"Minas Gerais"
```

```{python}
#| tags: [parameters]
UF = "Minas Gerais"
```

## Setup

```{python}
from datetime import date
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandera.polars as pa
import polars as pl
import seaborn as sns
from IPython.display import Markdown
from scipy import stats
from statsforecast import StatsForecast
from statsforecast.arima import ndiffs, nsdiffs
from statsforecast.models import AutoARIMA
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf, plot_pacf
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox
from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL
from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller, kpss

SEASON = 12  # monthly data
HORIZON = 24  # months ahead
LEVELS = [80, 95]

# Okabe-Ito: colorblind-safe categorical palette
OKABE_ITO = [
    "#E69F00",
    "#56B4E9",
    "#009E73",
    "#F0E442",
    "#0072B2",
    "#D55E00",
    "#CC79A7",
]
BLUE, ORANGE, VERMILION, GREY = "#0072B2", "#E69F00", "#D55E00", "#6B6B6B"
sns.set_theme(style="ticks", palette=OKABE_ITO)
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})

# Show whole tables, without polars' shape and dtype header rows
pl.Config.set_tbl_rows(-1)
pl.Config.set_tbl_hide_dataframe_shape(True)
pl.Config.set_tbl_hide_column_data_types(True)
pl.Config.set_fmt_str_lengths(80)


def correlogram(
    values: np.ndarray, ax: plt.Axes, kind: str = "acf", lags: int = 36
) -> None:
    """ACF or PACF with a neutral significance band and the seasonal lags marked."""
    plotter = plot_acf if kind == "acf" else plot_pacf
    extra = {} if kind == "acf" else {"method": "ywm"}
    plotter(
        values,
        lags=lags,
        ax=ax,
        title=kind.upper(),
        color=BLUE,
        vlines_kwargs={"colors": BLUE},
        **extra,
    )
    # statsmodels fills the band with the next palette color; grey keeps it
    # from reading as data
    for band in ax.collections[1:]:
        band.set_facecolor(GREY)
        band.set_alpha(0.15)
    for lag in range(SEASON, lags + 1, SEASON):
        ax.axvline(lag, color=VERMILION, lw=0.6, ls=":")
```

## Loading the PMC data

The CSV is downloaded once and cached as Parquet in `data/raw/`, so the report re-renders the
same way even if the GitHub release is unavailable. Parquet also keeps the `Date` type.

```{python}
DATA_URL = (
    "https://github.com/padsInsper/202634-fa/releases/download/data/pmc_volume_uf.csv"
)
CACHE = Path("data/raw/pmc_volume_uf.parquet")

if CACHE.exists():
    pmc = pl.read_parquet(CACHE)
else:
    pmc = pl.read_csv(DATA_URL).with_columns(pl.col("data").str.to_date("%Y-%m-%d"))
    CACHE.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    pmc.write_parquet(CACHE)

valid_ufs = pmc["uf"].unique().sort().to_list()
if UF not in valid_ufs:
    raise ValueError(f"UF {UF!r} is not in the data. Valid values: {valid_ufs}")

# Nixtla long format: unique_id, ds, y
df_sf = (
    pmc.filter(pl.col("uf") == UF)
    .select(
        pl.col("uf").alias("unique_id"),
        pl.col("data").alias("ds"),
        pl.col("volume_idx").cast(pl.Float64).alias("y"),
    )
    .sort("ds")
)
df_sf.head()
```

Before modeling, a data-quality check: a missing or duplicated month would silently shift
every seasonal lag, so it is better to fail loudly here.

```{python}
class MonthlySeries(pa.DataFrameModel):
    """One row per month: first-of-month dates, no gaps, no duplicates, finite y."""

    unique_id: str
    ds: pl.Date = pa.Field(unique=True)
    y: pl.Float64 = pa.Field(nullable=False)

    @pa.check("ds", name="month_start")
    def month_start(cls, data: pa.PolarsData) -> pl.LazyFrame:
        return data.lazyframe.select(pl.col(data.key).dt.day() == 1)

    @pa.check("y", name="finite")
    def finite(cls, data: pa.PolarsData) -> pl.LazyFrame:
        return data.lazyframe.select(pl.col(data.key).is_finite())

    @pa.dataframe_check(name="no_missing_months")
    def no_gaps(cls, data: pa.PolarsData) -> pl.LazyFrame:
        months = pl.col("ds").dt.year() * 12 + pl.col("ds").dt.month()
        return data.lazyframe.select(months.diff().fill_null(1) == 1)


df_sf = MonthlySeries.validate(df_sf)
first, last = df_sf["ds"].min(), df_sf["ds"].max()
Markdown(
    f"**State (UF): {UF}** · {df_sf.height} months, "
    f"{first:%b %Y} to {last:%b %Y} · data checks passed."
)
```

## Descriptive analysis

### The series

The 12-month centered moving average removes the seasonal cycle, which makes the trend easier
to see. It is only for this picture: a centered window looks into the future, so it must never
be used as a model feature.

```{python}
plot_df = df_sf.with_columns(
    pl.col("y").rolling_mean(window_size=SEASON, center=True).alias("ma12")
)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(plot_df["ds"], plot_df["y"], color=BLUE, lw=1, label="Volume index")
ax.plot(
    plot_df["ds"], plot_df["ma12"], color=ORANGE, lw=2, label="12-month moving average"
)
ax.axhline(100, color=GREY, lw=0.8, ls=":")
ax.set(
    title=f"Expanded retail sales volume, {UF}",
    ylabel="Index (2022 = 100)",
    xlabel=None,
)
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

### Decomposition (STL)

STL is the course's recommended decomposition (`aulas/fundamentos.qmd`). `robust=True` keeps
one-off shocks such as April 2020 in the remainder instead of distorting the seasonal pattern.

```{python}
y = df_sf["y"].to_numpy()
dates = df_sf["ds"].to_list()
stl = STL(y, period=SEASON, robust=True).fit()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 1, figsize=(10, 8), sharex=True)
for ax, values, name in zip(
    axes,
    [y, stl.trend, stl.seasonal, stl.resid],
    ["Observed", "Trend", "Seasonal", "Remainder"],
    strict=True,
):
    ax.plot(dates, values, color=BLUE, lw=1)
    ax.set_ylabel(name)
axes[3].axhline(0, color=GREY, lw=0.8)
fig.suptitle("STL decomposition (robust)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Strength of trend and seasonality (Wang, Smith & Hyndman 2006). AutoARIMA's
# seasonal test applies a seasonal difference when seasonal strength > 0.64.
var_r = np.var(stl.resid)
trend_strength = max(0.0, 1 - var_r / np.var(stl.trend + stl.resid))
seasonal_strength = max(0.0, 1 - var_r / np.var(stl.seasonal + stl.resid))
Markdown(
    f"Trend strength: **{trend_strength:.2f}** · "
    f"seasonal strength: **{seasonal_strength:.2f}** (threshold 0.64)."
)
```

### Seasonal pattern by month

The boxplot shows which months are consistently above or below the trend, and how stable
that effect is across years. It uses the **detrended** series (observed minus the STL trend):
on raw levels, each box would mostly show the trend (the index roughly doubled over the
sample), hiding the seasonal effect.

```{python}
by_month = df_sf.with_columns(
    (pl.col("y") - pl.Series(stl.trend)).alias("detrended"),
    pl.col("ds").dt.strftime("%b").alias("month"),
)
month_order = [f"{date(2000, m, 1):%b}" for m in range(1, 13)]
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.boxplot(
    data=by_month.to_pandas(),
    x="month",
    y="detrended",
    order=month_order,
    color=OKABE_ITO[1],
    ax=ax,
)
ax.axhline(0, color=GREY, lw=0.8)
ax.set(
    title="Seasonal effect: detrended index by calendar month",
    xlabel=None,
    ylabel="Index points above / below trend",
)
plt.show()
```

### ACF and PACF: original series and differences

Seasonal difference first, then the regular difference (`aulas/arima.qmd`). If you take the
regular difference first, a strong seasonal cycle can be mistaken for trend.

```{python}
diffs = df_sf.select(
    pl.col("y"),
    pl.col("y").diff(SEASON).alias("y_d12"),
    pl.col("y").diff(SEASON).diff(1).alias("y_d1_d12"),
)
series = {
    "Original": diffs["y"].to_numpy(),
    "Seasonal difference (Δ₁₂)": diffs["y_d12"].drop_nulls().to_numpy(),
    "Seasonal + regular difference (ΔΔ₁₂)": diffs["y_d1_d12"].drop_nulls().to_numpy(),
}

# mathtext for the titles: the plot font has no Unicode subscript glyphs
plot_titles = [
    "Original",
    r"Seasonal difference ($\Delta_{12}$)",
    r"Seasonal + regular difference ($\Delta\Delta_{12}$)",
]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(12, 9))
for row, title, values in zip(axes, plot_titles, series.values(), strict=True):
    row[0].plot(dates[len(dates) - len(values) :], values, color=BLUE, lw=0.9)
    row[0].set_title(title, fontsize=10, loc="left")
    correlogram(values, row[1], "acf")
    correlogram(values, row[2], "pacf")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The dotted vertical lines mark the seasonal lags (12, 24, 36). Read them separately from the
short lags 1 to 3: the short lags suggest p and q, and the seasonal lags suggest P and Q
(`aulas/sarima-prophet.qmd`).

## Unit root tests

The two tests have **opposite null hypotheses**, so they are read together
(`aulas/fundamentos.qmd`):

| ADF (H0: unit root) | KPSS (H0: stationary) | Conclusion |
|---|---|---|
| rejects | does not reject | stationary |
| does not reject | rejects | unit root: difference |
| both reject | | inconclusive (possibly trend-stationary) |
| neither rejects | | inconclusive |

```{python}
def joint_verdict(adf_p: float, kpss_p: float, alpha: float = 0.05) -> str:
    """Joint reading of ADF and KPSS, as in the course table."""
    adf_rejects, kpss_rejects = adf_p < alpha, kpss_p < alpha
    if adf_rejects and not kpss_rejects:
        return "stationary"
    if kpss_rejects and not adf_rejects:
        return "unit root: difference"
    return "inconclusive"


def fmt_kpss_p(p: float) -> str:
    """statsmodels truncates KPSS p-values to the [0.01, 0.10] table range."""
    if p <= 0.01:
        return "≤ 0.01"
    if p >= 0.10:
        return "≥ 0.10"
    return f"{p:.3f}"


rows = []
for name, values in series.items():
    adf_stat, adf_p, *_ = adfuller(values, autolag="AIC")
    kpss_stat, kpss_p, *_ = kpss(values, regression="c", nlags="auto")
    rows.append(
        {
            "series": name,
            "ADF stat": round(adf_stat, 2),
            "ADF p-value": round(adf_p, 3),
            "KPSS stat": round(kpss_stat, 2),
            "KPSS p-value": fmt_kpss_p(kpss_p),
            "joint reading (5%)": joint_verdict(adf_p, kpss_p),
        }
    )
pl.DataFrame(rows)
```

`ndiffs` and `nsdiffs` estimate the number of differences automatically, using the same tests
AutoARIMA uses internally: a seasonal-strength test for D, then KPSS on the seasonally
differenced series for d.

```{python}
D_hat = nsdiffs(y, period=SEASON)
y_seasonal = y[SEASON * D_hat :] - y[: len(y) - SEASON * D_hat] if D_hat else y
d_hat = ndiffs(y_seasonal)
Markdown(
    f"`nsdiffs` → **D = {D_hat}** seasonal difference(s) · "
    f"`ndiffs` → **d = {d_hat}** regular difference(s)."
)
```

## Modeling: AutoARIMA

`AutoARIMA(season_length=12)` chooses D and d with the tests above, then searches over p, q, P
and Q step by step, keeping the model with the lowest AICc. It is "a tool, not an answer"
(`aulas/arima.qmd`), so the residual diagnostics below decide whether the model can be trusted.

```{python}
sf = StatsForecast(models=[AutoARIMA(season_length=SEASON)], freq="1mo", n_jobs=1)
sf.fit(df_sf)
model = sf.fitted_[0, 0].model_

# statsforecast stores the orders as (p, q, P, Q, s, d, D)
p, q, P, Q, s, d, D = model["arma"]
order_label = f"SARIMA({p},{d},{q})({P},{D},{Q})[{s}]"
coefs = pl.DataFrame(
    {
        "term": list(model["coef"]),
        "estimate": [round(v, 4) for v in model["coef"].values()],
    }
)
Markdown(
    f"Selected model: **{order_label}** · AICc = {model['aicc']:.1f} · "
    f"σ² = {model['sigma2']:.2f}"
)
```

```{python}
coefs
```

## Residual diagnostics

The residuals should behave like white noise. In order of priority: no autocorrelation,
constant variance, and (desirable but not essential) normality. The first `d + D·s`
residuals come from the differencing start-up period, so they are dropped.

```{python}
burn_in = d + D * s
resid = np.asarray(model["residuals"])[burn_in:]
resid_dates = dates[burn_in:]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
axes[0, 0].plot(resid_dates, resid, color=BLUE, lw=0.9)
axes[0, 0].axhline(0, color=GREY, lw=0.8)
axes[0, 0].set_title("Residuals over time", loc="left")

correlogram(resid, axes[0, 1], "acf")
axes[0, 1].set_title("")
axes[0, 1].set_title("Residual ACF", loc="left")

sns.histplot(resid, stat="density", color=OKABE_ITO[1], ax=axes[1, 0])
grid = np.linspace(resid.min(), resid.max(), 200)
axes[1, 0].plot(
    grid,
    stats.norm.pdf(grid, resid.mean(), resid.std()),
    color=VERMILION,
    label="Normal",
)
axes[1, 0].set_title("Distribution vs normal", loc="left")
axes[1, 0].legend(frameon=False)

stats.probplot(resid, dist="norm", plot=axes[1, 1])
axes[1, 1].get_lines()[0].set(color=BLUE, markersize=3)
axes[1, 1].get_lines()[1].set(color=VERMILION)
axes[1, 1].set_title("")  # drop scipy's default "Probability Plot" title
axes[1, 1].set_title("Normal Q-Q", loc="left")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Ljung-Box tests whether the first *h* autocorrelations are jointly zero. **H0 is white noise,
so a high p-value is the good result.** `model_df = p + q + P + Q` removes the degrees of
freedom used by the fitted ARMA terms (`aulas/arima.qmd`).

```{python}
lb = acorr_ljungbox(resid, lags=[12, 24, 36], model_df=p + q + P + Q)
ljung_box = pl.from_pandas(lb.reset_index(names="lag")).with_columns(
    pl.col("lb_stat").round(2),
    pl.col("lb_pvalue").round(4),
    pl.when(pl.col("lb_pvalue") > 0.05)
    .then(pl.lit("consistent with white noise"))
    .otherwise(pl.lit("autocorrelation remains"))
    .alias("reading (5%)"),
)
jb_stat, jb_p = stats.jarque_bera(resid)
ljung_box
```

## Forecast: 24 months ahead

```{python}
fc = sf.predict(h=HORIZON, level=LEVELS)
fc_cols = {
    "mean": "AutoARIMA",
    **{
        f"{side}_{lv}": f"AutoARIMA-{side}-{lv}"
        for lv in LEVELS
        for side in ("lo", "hi")
    },
}

history = df_sf.filter(pl.col("ds") >= pl.date(last.year - 7, 1, 1))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 5))
ax.plot(history["ds"], history["y"], color=GREY, lw=1.2, label="History")
ax.fill_between(
    fc["ds"],
    fc[fc_cols["lo_95"]],
    fc[fc_cols["hi_95"]],
    color=BLUE,
    alpha=0.15,
    lw=0,
    label="95% interval",
)
ax.fill_between(
    fc["ds"],
    fc[fc_cols["lo_80"]],
    fc[fc_cols["hi_80"]],
    color=BLUE,
    alpha=0.30,
    lw=0,
    label="80% interval",
)
ax.plot(fc["ds"], fc[fc_cols["mean"]], color=BLUE, lw=2, label="Forecast")
ax.axvline(last, color=GREY, lw=0.8, ls=":")
ax.set(ylabel="Index (2022 = 100)", xlabel=None)
ax.set_title(f"{order_label}: {HORIZON}-month forecast, {UF}", pad=30)
# legend in one row above the plot, so it never covers the data
ax.legend(frameon=False, ncols=4, loc="lower left", bbox_to_anchor=(0, 1.0))
plt.show()
```

The forecast is drawn as a fan chart: two nested bands, with the darker 80% band inside the
95% band, so the uncertainty reads as part of the forecast instead of an extra line. Only the
last 7 years of history are shown, so the forecast period is not squeezed into the right edge.

```{python}
forecast_table = fc.select(
    pl.col("ds").dt.strftime("%Y-%m").alias("month"),
    *[pl.col(c).round(1).alias(k) for k, c in fc_cols.items()],
).with_columns((pl.col("hi_95") - pl.col("lo_95")).round(1).alias("width_95"))
forecast_table
```

## Discussion

### Evidence to support your answers

These numbers come straight from the analysis above. The interpretation is yours.

```{python}
width = forecast_table["width_95"]
resid_acf = np.array([np.corrcoef(resid[:-k], resid[k:])[0, 1] for k in (12, 24)])
band = 1.96 / np.sqrt(len(resid))
lb_pvalues = " / ".join(f"{v:.3f}" for v in lb["lb_pvalue"])
worst = np.abs(resid).argmax()

evidence = [
    f"- **Seasonality / trend (STL):** seasonal strength {seasonal_strength:.2f}, "
    f"trend strength {trend_strength:.2f}.",
    f"- **Differences:** `nsdiffs` D = {D_hat}, `ndiffs` d = {d_hat}; "
    f"AutoARIMA used d = {d}, D = {D}.",
    f"- **Selected model:** {order_label}, with AR terms p = {p}, P = {P} "
    f"and MA terms q = {q}, Q = {Q}.",
    f"- **Ljung-Box p-values** (lags 12/24/36): {lb_pvalues}.",
    f"- **Residual autocorrelation at seasonal lags:** "
    f"lag 12 = {resid_acf[0]:.2f}, lag 24 = {resid_acf[1]:.2f} "
    f"(95% band ±{band:.2f}).",
    f"- **Normality (Jarque-Bera):** p = {jb_p:.3g}; largest absolute residual "
    f"{abs(resid[worst]):.1f} in {resid_dates[worst]:%b %Y}.",
    f"- **95% interval width:** {width[0]:.1f} at h = 1, "
    f"{width[11]:.1f} at h = 12, {width[23]:.1f} at h = 24 points.",
]
Markdown("\n".join(evidence))
```

## Check your intuition for question 5 (open after answering)

The same `AutoARIMA(season_length=12)` fitted to every state.

```{python}
all_ufs = pmc.select(
    pl.col("uf").alias("unique_id"),
    pl.col("data").alias("ds"),
    pl.col("volume_idx").cast(pl.Float64).alias("y"),
).sort("unique_id", "ds")
sf_all = StatsForecast(models=[AutoARIMA(season_length=SEASON)], freq="1mo", n_jobs=1)
sf_all.fit(all_ufs)

rows = []
for uid, fitted in zip(sf_all.uids, sf_all.fitted_[:, 0], strict=True):
    p_, q_, P_, Q_, s_, d_, D_ = fitted.model_["arma"]
    rows.append(
        {
            "UF": uid,
            "model": f"({p_},{d_},{q_})({P_},{D_},{Q_})[{s_}]",
            "AICc": round(fitted.model_["aicc"], 1),
        }
    )
pl.DataFrame(rows).with_columns((pl.col("UF") == UF).alias("yours"))
```

:::
